title: Lindsey Buckingham, Madison Beer, Kiernan Shipka and Tiffani Thiessen Named As Presenters for Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood
description: Variety has announced presenters for its annual Power of Young Hollywood, this year presented by Disney+, taking place on Aug. 5 in Los Angeles. Pre
body:
Variety has announced presenters for its annual Power of Young Hollywood, this year presented by Disney+, taking place on Aug. 5 in Los Angeles. Presenting Tate McRae with the Triple Threat Award will be Madison Beer, and presenting Sombr with the Songwriter of the Year award is Lindsey Buckingham. Tyriq Withers will receive the New Leading Man Award from Kiernan Shipka, and Malachi Barton will be presented the Rising Star Award by Tiffani Thiessen.
	

	The event will be cohosted by Mario Lopez and his son Dominic. A two-time Emmy winner, Mario Lopez hosts NBC’s “Access Hollywood” and “Access Daily” concurrently with the national iHeart radio programs “On with Mario & Courtney Lopez” and “iHeartRadio Countdown with Mario Lopez.” His son, Dominic Lopez, is a rising young actor who can be seen on CBS’s “Matlock,” Netflix’s “The Lincoln Lawyer” and indie films “Bad Counselors” and “Last Shot.” Mario and Dominic will star together alongside Tony Danza in the upcoming holiday film “Christmas at Starlight.”


	A two-time Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter, Beer recently concluded her 32-date Locket Tour across Europe and North America following the release of her deluxe album “Locket” earlier this summer. Beer got her start posting viral covers on YouTube and has since released an EP and three studio albums, the second of which earned her her first Grammy nomination for Best Immersive Audio Album in 2024. In 2025, she was nominated again for her single “Make You Mine,” for which she also won Pop-Dance Anthem of the Year at the Electronic Music Dance Awards.
	

	Joining Fleetwood Mac in 1975 as guitarist, co-lead singer and later, producer, Buckingham helped turn the band into one of the greatest stories in music with their 1977 album “Rumours,” one of the best-selling albums of all time. Beyond Fleetwood Mac, Buckingham has released several solo albums showcasing his experimental production style, including “Law and Order”, ‘’Go Insane’’ and “Gift of Screws”. Buckingham was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Fleetwood Mac in 1998.

	Shipka first gained widespread recognition as Sally Draper on AMC’s “Mad Men” before starring as Sabrina Spellman in Netflix’s “Chilling Adventures of Sabrina.” Since then, she has built a distinctive career across film and television. Her recent credits include “Longlegs,” “Twisters,” “The Last Showgirl,” and HBO’s” Industry.” She will next be seen in “Idiots,” directed by Macon Blair, alongside Dave Franco, O’Shea Jackson Jr., and Mason Thames. The film premiered at the Sundance Film Festival and opens in theaters on August 28.

	Thiessen is known for her iconic role as Kelly Kapowski on “Saved by the Bell,” as well as roles on “White Collar” and “Alexa & Katie,” for which she earned a Daytime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Supporting Actress. Thiessen, along with honoree Barton, will be starring in the upcoming supernatural comedy-drama “Coven Academy” on Disney Channel and Disney+.

	For the first time in the event’s history, Variety‘s Power of Young Hollywood will feature a live musical performance, presented by Amazon Music’s Breakthrough program. Amazon Music’s newest Breakthrough artist, acclaimed singer-songwriter Sienna Spiro, will perform “Pure” from her debut album, “Visitor,” ahead of her sold-out global headline “My House” tour kicking off this fall.

	Disney+ is the presenting partner of this year’s Power of Young Hollywood party. Neutrogena is the Official Skincare Partner. Cash App is a premier partner, Amazon Music is the official performance sponsor, HYBE is an official sponsor, Eternal Water is the official water partner and Untitled is a supporting sponsor.

title: Inside Google’s Efforts to Get Creatives Hooked on AI
description:

body:
I was about 15 minutes into Google’s AI short-film screening when I realized I had nearly finished my popcorn.

	Granted, the bag was small. But the rapid munching was a natural consequence of my piqued intrigue late last month as the tech giant showcased 11 AI-generated short films at Manhattan’s arthouse Metrograph theater. The directors — a mix of various ages, demographics and professional backgrounds — were the fourth cohort in Google’s “Flow Sessions” program, a six-week intensive that gives a group of up-and-coming filmmakers unlimited access to the company’s Flow short-form AI video generator and several mentorship sessions to bring a short story idea to life. 
	

	It’s no secret that short-form videos have been a layman’s doorway into moviemaking in the AI era, with companies luring users with the notion of bringing their imaginations to life in ways unfathomable before the advent of generators. Google knows this as well, and the short-film exhibition seems as designed to present the films and the technology as it does to showcase the company’s eagerness for the film industry to embrace AI’s potential, moves further reflected in its DeepMind research partnership with A24 and its work with filmmakers including Darren Aronofsky and Doug Liman.


	That includes hiring a filmmaker-in-residence, Henry Daubrez, who has worked with each cohort to shepherd their ideas from concept to generated reality. Daubrez says the AI era means one doesn’t need a professionally creative background to tell stories, as those from other industries have found a pathway to tell stories that would’ve otherwise lain dormant in their minds.
	

	“Life is messy,” he tells me in a video interview ahead of the latest screening. “Sometimes that was my dream career, and they get there. Sometimes they had [a dream] and it didn’t work out. Sometimes they had to keep in the family business. I think what AI is doing — and I understand the pushback about most people can say, ‘Hey, you have a camera on your phone. What prevents you from going outside and shooting?’ Depends what you want to say — the story, VFX is expensive, it’s still complicated to put things together. But I think for a lot of people, it’s gonna give them a new door.”

	It’s a sentiment Google’s keen to put out there, from the cast of creators they’ve enlisted to the venue they’ve chosen. The sessions’ screening venue moved from Tribeca’s Roxy Cinema to the much bigger Metrograph in the Lower East Side, an ode to the cinephile demographic that reveres the theater. (A prior July event at Metrograph: Charli xcx’s early listening event for her latest album “Music, Fashion, Film.”)

	But it’s one that still contrasts with the industry consternation around AI generators, which studios and creative unions have still torn into for scraping copyrighted content without creators’ consent. Such concerns remain evident in some of this cohort’s films themselves — the screening of the meditation-focused short ”One Breath at a Time,” by director Santiago Carrasquilla, featured a prominent shot of a Nintendo Game Boy logo that was promptly blurred for its online release. (Google never explicitly banned logos from the shorts, one director told me, though it was suggested they blur them.)

	The short films themselves ran the gamut from the abstract to the questionable, with layers of emotion sprinkled in throughout the hourlong session. One, “Two Chairs,” dove into director Dion Lee’s existential crisis over whether to have children, with AI aiding in animated sequences. It’s a story rooted in emotion, a far cry from the wholly AI-generated, “Texas Chainsaw Massacre”-inspired horror short “Mascot,” which featured a costumed character in Times Square assaulting a man who didn’t pay for the photos he took of them. Another short, “Nothin’ Beats a Cheeseburger,” revolved around an alien arriving on Earth to indulge in the alleged “world’s best cheeseburger,” using real actors for the two leads while AI generated the alien’s likeness onto one of them.
	

	The credits for “Mascot” featured behind-the-scenes shots of the two characters — the violent costumer and the frightened photographer — that made me question whether its director, short-form filmmaker Daniel Garcia, took a hybrid approach of real actors within AI sequences. But those shots, too, were also wholly AI, a choice Garcia says was a cheeky choice to lampoon those interested in how films are made but one that left me worried over whether it clouded reality.

	“Seeing is not believing anymore,” he says. “So I just thought that, especially with AI, the behind-the-scenes is more important than the actual product. And I think now, because everyone has access to the tools, everyone can make cinematic stories easily, and what I find now is that most people are not interested in the actual film. They’re more interested in how you made it.”

	Still, humanity emerged in Lee’s film, which physically featured the 35-year-old creative director in the six-minute project as she wrote letters to her future self and potential daughter. Lee tells me it was paramount she starred in the film because of its personal nature. “It would be weird if it was someone else,” she says.

	Lee, a freelance art director who’s worked everywhere from Vox.com to the New York Times, says over drinks at the post-screening reception how she uses AI models to help generate assets, such as, in “Two Chairs,” a chair. But she understood people’s hesitancy toward the technology and doesn’t believe it needs to be forced upon those who aren’t already eager to embrace it.

	“I think it’s good for things that you need but you can’t necessarily have access to on a day-to-day basis, and if you’re happy with that, then that’s great,” she says. “If you don’t need that or want that, then that’s totally fine too. I just feel like take what you can from it. It’s a tool. If it doesn’t work for you, then it doesn’t work for you.”

	Still, Lee says she’d use AI to help produce other video projects, suggesting Google’s gambit — whether embraced by Hollywood or not – may pay off.

title: LISTEN: National Comedy Center’s Journey Gunderson on Preserving Humor as History
description: On today’s episode of “Daily Variety” podcast, Journey Gunderson, executive director of the National Comedy Center in Jamestown, N.Y., explains why
body:
On today’s episode of “Daily Variety” podcast, Journey Gunderson, executive director of the National Comedy Center in Jamestown, N.Y., explains why it’s important to have an institution devoted to the study of comedy. Jamestown, which is the hometown of Lucille Ball, will be abuzz with laughs as the center hosts the annual Lucille Ball Comedy Festival Aug. 6-9, headlined by Jerry Seinfeld, Bert Kreischer and Seth Meyers.

	Gunderson has been the driving force behind the nonprofit National Comedy Center for 15 years. She joined what was then the Lucille Ball Desi Arnaz Museum in Jamestown in 2011. In 2018, the organization’s footprint expanded to include the National Comedy Center, which is now home to the archives of comedy titans George Carlin, Carl Reiner and Mel Brooks.
	

	The lure of working in Lucy’s hometown has been strong for A-list comedians for decades, as the comedy festival predated the launch of the center. But nowadays, when top stars parachute in for the festival, they’re able to tour the center and recognize that it is unique among museums and cultural institutions.

	“I do think that sets us apart from any other city that an artist is touring and performing within. And the word has gotten out in the artist community that you have to make ample time to traverse the galleries of the National Comedy Center when you come and perform at the Lucille Ball Comedy Festival in Jamestown,” Gunderson says. “My favorite part of the job is touring the comedians themselves. When Jon Stewart toured the museum before headlining the festival last year, he just said, ‘No one’s ever done this for us before. No one has done this.’ I think it felt profound to him — the realization as he was walking through the museum that it wasn’t until 2018 that anybody opened a museum that tells the story of this art form.”
	

	The festival draws visitors from around the country, many of whom travel distances to attend. The momentum that the event has generated in recent years has helped propel the center to new prominence. And that is reinforced by the fact that a living legend such as Brooks has committed his papers and memorabilia to the center.

	“We knew there was a void of anybody taking responsibility for conservation and preservation in this way. Most people agree that comedy history is important, but also assume that important things somehow get saved automatically and they don’t. Preservation does not happen passively,” Gunderson says. “Someone has to decide to preserve something before it’s lost. And that is why we built the National Archive. There’s an urgency to this conservation work as well, so that it can be around for future generations to learn from.”

	Brooks’ archive alone includes more than 150,000 documents and more than 5,000 photographs. Most important, it offers a window into how his comedy developed over time and how the world around him shaped his unique brand of yucks.

	“From a very early age, Mel Brooks knew how to wield comedy to take back power. His ability to fearlessly satirize the atrocities of war and the horrors of humanity not only helped heal a post-World War II nation, it’s a playbook we want future generations to have. This is a method of processing. It’s a method of grieving. But it’s also a way of taking power back from a situation. And Mel Brooks could blend what some might consider lowbrow slapstick with highbrow satire like no other. And I’m glad he’s still doing it to this day.”

	(Pictured: Jon Stewart tours the National Comedy Center with executive director Journey Gunderson in 2025)

	Listen to Daily Variety on iHeartPodcasts, Apple Podcasts, Variety’s YouTube Podcast channel, Amazon Music, Spotify and other podcast platforms.

schema.headline: LISTEN: National Comedy Center’s Journey Gunderson on Preserving Humor as History

title: Naomi Watts’ Secret ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Role Reunited Her With Tom Holland, 12 Years After ‘The Impossible’: ‘From Playing Your Mom to Your AI’
description: Naomi Watts has taken to Instagram to celebrate her secret role in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” Sony and Marvel Studios’ record-breaking superhero m
body:
Naomi Watts has taken to Instagram to celebrate her secret role in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” Sony and Marvel Studios’ record-breaking superhero movie. The Oscar nominee voices Peter Parker’s artificial intelligence assistant E.V. in the movie. Watts celebrated the film’s success on social media while sharing a photo of herself recording her lines virtually with “Brand New Day” director Destin Daniel Cretton.

	“From playing your mom to playing your AI (100% human made),” Watts wrote in the caption. “Congrats Tom [Holland], Destin, and the whole ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ team on the historic opening weekend!! Immensely proud to even just a tiny part of this incredible film!”
	

	Watts’ voice role in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” reunited her with Cretton, Holland and Sadie Sink. Not only did she star in Cretton’s 2017 drama “The Glass Castle” alongside sink and fellow MCU alum Brie Larson, but Watts and Holland graced the screen in 2012’s “The Impossible.” The movie, a harrowing account of one family’s separation during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, earned Watts an Oscar nomination for best actress and marked Holland’s acting debut in a live-action feature film. 


	During Holland’s press tour for “The Odyssey” and “Brand New Day,” he stopped by Amy Poehler’s “Good Hang” podcast and praised Watts for being the first person to teach him how to conduct himself on a film set when they made “The Impossible” together. Holland said that through Watts he was able to “watch a professional at the top of her game deliver, you know, a sort of masterful performance while also taking me under her wing and teaching me everything I know about cinema.”
	

	Holland landed the role of Peter Parker/Spider-Man three years after “The Impossible.” Now him and Watts are back on screen interacting together in “Brand New Day,” which set the domestic box office opening weekend record with a $360 million debut. The movie has grossed $1 billion globally in six days, becoming the second fastest film in history to hit the milestone. 

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is now playing in theaters nationwide.

schema.headline: Naomi Watts’ Secret ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Role Reunited Her With Tom Holland, 12 Years After ‘The Impossible’: ‘From Playing Your Mom to Your AI’

title: Cannibalism Comedy-Horror ‘Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,’ Starring Amir Nafis, Signs Abnormal Studios for Worldwide Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Kuala Lumpur genre outfit Abnormal Studios has taken on worldwide international sales for “Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,” a Malaysian cannibal black come
body:
Kuala Lumpur genre outfit Abnormal Studios has taken on worldwide international sales for “Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,” a Malaysian cannibal black comedy-horror from sibling filmmakers Iskander and Feisal Azizuddin. 

	The company plans to launch the title at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) in Busan this October.

	The ninth independent feature from the pair – working under their Feisk Productions banner – centers on two down-on-their-luck friends who accidentally hit upon a winning spicy beef jerky recipe – one with a distinctly human ingredient – and find their fortunes, and their moral compasses, spinning wildly out of control as the business takes off.
	

	Amir Nafis, one of Malaysia’s better-known screen actors, leads the cast alongside Syazani Zikry and Bella Imani. Original hand-drawn illustrations by Gladys Lee and Qistina Ishak feature throughout as visual storytelling elements.


	Co-director Feisal Azizuddin said: “I wanted to tell a story that explores how desperation warps ordinary people, and how ambition often wears a friendly face, and that we are another person’s dish in this complex, twisted society we live in.”

	The film takes cannibalism – rarely broached in Malaysian popular cinema – as both literal premise and social metaphor, training its lens on characters pushed to extremes by poverty and ambition. Where mainstream local filmmaking tends toward restraint, this picture pursues the opposite: explicit violence, sexuality and dark humor treated as formal choices rather than shock tactics, marking out a more transgressive current within contemporary Malaysian independent film.
	

	The Azizuddin Brothers have spent the better part of a decade making work that sidesteps genre convention and mainstream expectation. Earlier features include the multi-character drama “Angkat,” the psychological thriller “Tafakur,” the period-inflected “This Land of Mine” and the horror entry “Kabus.” “Angkat” screened at the 2024 Blue Chair Film Festival in Luang Prabang, Laos, where it received its world premiere. More recently, Feisk Productions cleared its crowdfunding target for “False Summits,” a documentary about a Malaysian mountaineer who died attempting Gunung Tahan, the tallest summit on the Malay Peninsula.

	Abnormal Studios, a Westec Media Limited subsidiary, brings roughly 100 titles a year to market across Southeast Asia as well as Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Mongolia and Nepal. Among its recent commercial successes are “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and “Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.”

	ACFM runs alongside the Busan International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Cannibalism Comedy-Horror ‘Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,’ Starring Amir Nafis, Signs Abnormal Studios for Worldwide Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Audrey Nuna Signs to Republic Records (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Audrey Nuna has signed to Republic Records in advance of her new single “superHuman,” Variety can exclusively reveal.

	The singer, who recently bro
body:
Audrey Nuna has signed to Republic Records in advance of her new single “superHuman,” Variety can exclusively reveal.

	The singer, who recently broke out as the voice of Mira in “KPop Demon Hunters,” worked with Grammy-winning producer Cirkut on “superHuman,” which releases at midnight ET this Friday. It marks her first release as part of her deal with Republic, which comes following a whirlwind year supporting “KPop Demon Hunters” that culminated in an Oscar win for best original song with Huntr/x’s “Golden” earlier this year.
	

	“I’m honored to work with a partner that believes in investing in the future of music and culture,” says Nuna about signing to Republic.


	“SuperHuman” introduces a new era for Nuna, who describes the track as a “portal.” “I wrote this song in a time in my life where a lot was changing very quickly, and I felt more perceived by the world than I ever had before,” she explains. “I wanted to capture that feeling – of redemption, of validation, of the tides finally turning. In the same breath, I wanted to quietly remind myself and others to stay human, stay open, to flow like water through all of the changes and that being more human will always be a superpower if we allow it.”

	Nuna also partnered with Riot Games for “superHuman” to be an official track for the 2026 Valorant Champions Tour (VCT), marking her second collaboration with Valorant following “Toxic” earlier this year.

	The 27-year-old has been on a hot streak in recent years following the launch of her music career in 2018 with indie tracks. She subsequently released two projects with Arista, most recently 2024’s “Trench,” before hitting full throttle as one-third of Huntr/x alongside Ejae and Rei Ami in 2025’s “KPop Demon Hunters.”
	

	Nuna is currently on a global festival run with performances lined up for Japan’s Summer Sonic 2026, Austria’s Frequency Festival and Belgium’s Pukkelpop through the end of the month.

schema.headline: Audrey Nuna Signs to Republic Records (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Hearst Clinches Deal to Buy Out A+E Global Media Stake From Disney for $1.2 Billion
description: Hearst has set a deal to acquire Disney’s 50% stake in A+E Global Media, the parent company of Lifetime, History Channel, A&E Network and other asse
body:
Hearst has set a deal to acquire Disney’s 50% stake in A+E Global Media, the parent company of Lifetime, History Channel, A&E Network and other assets in a deal that calls for Hearst to pay Disney $1.2 billion in cash.

	Disney and Hearst have been 50-50 partners in A+E Global Media for more than a decade. Hearst also owns a roughly 18% stake in Disney’s ESPN but that is separate from A+E Global Media and unaffected by the transaction. The A+E Global Media deal is expected to close in September, with Paul Buccieri remaining at the helm as president and chairman. 
	

	The deal puts Hearst back into national media in a big way. The company has deep roots in newspaper and magazine publishing and it operates a strong group of 35 local TV stations, most of them Big Three network affiliates. 


	“We thank our Disney colleagues for decades of successful partnership,” said Steven R. Swartz, president and CEO of Hearst. “We look forward to supporting Paul Buccieri and A+E Global Media’s leadership team as they continue to make must-see programs and innovate around the great History, Lifetime and A&E brands.”



	

					Paul Buccieri
									Courtesy of Paul Buccieri / Jeff Katz Photography
	



	The deal brings A+E Global Media full circle with Hearst taking full control of the assets. Hearst and Disney put the company on the block in July 2025. Starz was among the outside media companies that took a look at the company but it’s unclear if they ever got to a formal bid stage. With Hearst coming in, the A+E Global Media team will settle in with an owner that they know well. 

	The list of linear channels included in the deal includes Lifetime Movie Network, FYI and Vice TV. The assets also encompass content units A+E Studios, A+E Factual Studio, A&E IndieFilms, A+E Global Media Digital as well as streaming apps, games, FAST channels, AVOD and subscription-video services Crime 360, Lifetime Movie Club and History Vault.
	

	A+E Global Media is one of many traditional media companies that has faced challenges amid a changing pay TV ecosystem. The company’s core revenue base is shrinking amid cord-cutting and the rise of streaming options. Under the leadership of Buccieri, A+E Global Media has been actively diversifying its operations with the addition of A+E Studios to produce high-end shows, such as the Netflix drama “The Lincoln Lawyer,” as well as through the launch of FAST channels and niche subscription video services.

	“In a media environment defined by fragmentation, A+E Global Media’s advantage is the strength and versatility of our brands, our strong partnerships and our vast library of owned assets,” said Buccieri. “As we continue extending our storytelling globally across all platforms with IP that travels to every screen and form-factor, we believe we are well suited for whatever opportunities may come next. I also want to express my deepest thanks to Hearst, The Walt Disney Company and to our board members — both recent and past — for their guidance and support over the years.”

	The company has its roots in the fertile ground of early 1980s cable in New York. A&E Network and Lifetime were launched in early 1984 at a time when the overall cable channel lineup was still pretty thin. History Channel followed in 1995. All three channels have yielded numerous spinoffs over the years.For its first 20 years, A&E Networks was jointly owned by ABC, NBC and Hearst. When Comcast acquired NBCUniversal from General Electric in 2011, the cable giant had to sell off its stake in what was then A&E Networks to comply with federal merger conditions.

schema.headline: Hearst Clinches Deal to Buy Out A+E Global Media Stake From Disney for $1.2 Billion

title: Cate Blanchett, Nina Hoss on the Friendship Driving ‘Elektra/Persona’ at London’s National Theatre: ‘There’s a Lot of Masking and Unmasking’
description: “Elektra/Persona,” the U.K. National Theatre production fusing Sophocles’ “Elektra” with Ingmar Bergman’s “Persona,” grew out of friendship rather t
body:
“Elektra/Persona,” the U.K. National Theatre production fusing Sophocles’ “Elektra” with Ingmar Bergman’s “Persona,” grew out of friendship rather than a directorial concept imposed after casting, according to director Benedict Andrews.

	Andrews, Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss spoke at a BFI Southbank conversation held ahead of the play’s run, moderated by “The Guardian” chief film critic Peter Bradshaw following a screening of a restored 35mm print of Bergman’s 1966 masterpiece.
	

	“Elektra/Persona” runs at the National Theatre’s Lyttelton Theatre from Aug. 19 to Oct. 10. In Sophocles’ “Elektra,” the title character mourns her father’s murder and waits for her brother, Orestes, to return and help her avenge it at the hands of their mother, Clytemnestra. In Bergman’s “Persona,” an actress, Elisabet, falls silent mid-performance and is sent to recuperate on a remote island, where a nurse, Alma, is assigned to care for her and the two women’s identities begin to blur. Andrews’ production stages “Elektra” in its first half and “Persona” in its second, with Blanchett and Hoss alternating between Elektra and Clytemnestra, and between Alma and Elisabet. The cast also includes Ella Lily Hyland. The production is staged by arrangement with Music Theatre International on behalf of the Ingmar Bergman Foundation.


	Andrews described the production’s structure, with Blanchett and Hoss playing all four roles across the evening and swapping nightly.

	“It wasn’t an idea of like, either Cate or Nina should be Elektra or Elisabet,” Andrews said. “You would cast it very differently; you’d cast an older Clytemnestra, arguably you’d cast a younger Alma. The idea that in this piece about doubling and mirroring, the idea that they should become each other, and literally that that idea is embedded into our production with them playing both the roles and swapping the roles nightly, that’s built into the muscles and the fabric of the production.”
	

	Andrews said the collision of the two source works was only part of what drove the project.

	“And so, I think the idea was then for us, beyond my fascination with the collision of these two pieces, the idea was born out of friendship, and the idea was born out of our delights in being in rehearsal rooms together, the things we bring out from each other in rehearsal rooms, the way that we all push each other and the text in rehearsal rooms, and the way that we share the idea of a rehearsal room being a search and an experiment,” Andrews said.

	Andrews also noted the extent of his history with his two leads. “Cate and I, I think this is our fourth time working together,” Andrews said. The pair’s previous collaborations include “The War of the Roses” (2009), “Big and Small” (2011-12) and “The Maids” (2013-14), staged with the Sydney Theatre Company. Andrews directed Hoss in “The Cherry Orchard” at the Donmar Warehouse in 2024.

	Andrews said his fascination with the pairing stemmed from Bergman’s own position at what he called the “hinge or intersection of theater and cinema” – the director ran Stockholm’s Dramaten theater while making “Persona,” stepping down the same year the film was released.

	“I felt you can’t – it’s difficult to stage ‘Persona’ in a way on its own, because it’s so singular, and in such a strange atmosphere,” Andrews said. “It’s like another planet, like a kind of vacuum. And the idea that it would have this counter-energy, this feral, muscular violence of the Greek drama format.”

	Bradshaw asked how the pair protected their mental health while juggling both plays and swapping parts nightly. “I had a breakdown today!” Blanchett said, drawing laughter from the audience. Both actors insisted they were fine, though Hoss said the two had turned to each other that afternoon and agreed neither could imagine doing the production with anyone else. Blanchett cut in that the sentiment applied “every afternoon,” to more laughter.

	Hoss said she does not approach the four roles as conventional characters, but as facets of “the same spirit,” with each actor’s choices reshaping what the other can do in turn.

	“There’s a lot of masking and unmasking,” Blanchett said. “We were talking today, too, about persona being a mask. The word persona. But that also, the ancient Greek word for actor comes from hypocrite: to reveal or to examine under a mask some form of truth, that’s often an uncomfortable truth. And of course, didn’t have any pejorative meaning at all then. But Clytemnestra wears as many masks as other people do. Even Elektra does, she wears the mask of grief, and who is she without that mask of grief? And Clytemnestra’s got her own grief, so there’s a bit of a ‘grief-off’ between the two women!”
	

	Bradshaw raised the ambiguity of the film’s central letter, in which Elisabet leaves an envelope open for Alma to read, and asked whether Bergman was showing a darker, more sadistic side of his heroine.

	“I think we are constantly in a state of knowing and not knowing simultaneously, wanting to hide and wanting to be revealed simultaneously,” Blanchett said. “I think that’s part of being alive.”

	Hoss offered a different account of the letter scene, characterizing it less as calculated cruelty than as an act of curiosity that shifts the power balance between the two women once Alma reads it.

	Andrews said the piece’s swapped-role structure demands generosity from both actors, requiring each to relinquish the instinct to defend her own character’s position within the mother-daughter conflict at the center of “Elektra.”

	BFI Fellow Blanchett was credited by Bradshaw with helping secure the 35mm print for two screenings that evening.

schema.headline: Cate Blanchett, Nina Hoss on the Friendship Driving ‘Elektra/Persona’ at London’s National Theatre: ‘There’s a Lot of Masking and Unmasking’

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Star Samantha Morton ‘Hasn’t Worked for a Year’ After Making Nolan’s Epic Because ‘I’m 49’ Years Old and ‘There’s Other Good Actors Out There’
description: Samantha Morton revealed on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast that she has been out of acting work for an entire year since wrapping production on Ch
body:
Samantha Morton revealed on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast that she has been out of acting work for an entire year since wrapping production on Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” in 2025. The two-time Oscar nominee attributed her age as the reason why. 

	“I haven’t worked for a year since making ‘The Odyssey,’ you know, and I’ve got really good agents and a manager, but at the end of the day, I’m 49,” Morton said. “I do believe I’m a good actor, [but] there are other good actors out there. Do you know what I mean? So, the politics of the industry has changed massively.”
	

	Morton said that when Nolan called her to offer her the role of the witch Circe in “The Odyssey” opposite Matt Damon that it afforded her “hope and faith, that, I suppose, if you keep at it, and you keep producing good work, and that the right people see it, then maybe you can carry on working.”


	The 49-year-old has been a working actor since 1991 and her career spans major Hollywood movies (Steven Spielberg’s “Minority Report”) and franchises (“The Walking Dead”) in addition to indie dramas that have garnered her Oscar nominations (“Sweet and Lowdown,” “In America”) and various awards. Morton has earned some of the best reviews of her career and Oscar buzz for playing Circe in “The Odyssey.” Variety ranked her as the movie’s best performance among the sprawling ensemble cast.

	“When I got the call [from Chris Nolan], I started to cry,” Morton previously told Variety about landing Circe. “Then we had a get to know you chat, and I read the script. But I didn’t know if it would go any further. So when he called and said, ‘Would you like to do it?’ I was blown away. He could have anybody on the planet, and he chose me… As you get older as an actress, roles like this are just few and far between.”
	

	Morton also opened up on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast about one of her lowest points as an actor, which is when she was dropped from Spike Jonze’s “Her” after filming already wrapped. Morton was the original voice of the chatbot Samantha, who Joaquin Phoenix’s character falls in love with. Morton read her lines aloud on set with Phoenix during production was booted from the movie and replaced by Scarlett Johansson in post production. 

	“I have to say, I think my version of Samantha was very… she’s English,” Morton said on the podcast. “It was just very, very different. And I think Scarlett Johansson has a beautiful voice. She’s incredibly evocative. It’s, you know… I got it, but I was sad… It does hurt when you’re fired from something or before it. I don’t know. What I’d have wished for was another chance in a booth to do an American accent. But I think, you know, Scarlett Johansson! I mean, come on.”

	Watch Morton’s full interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” in the video below.

schema.headline: ‘The Odyssey’ Star Samantha Morton ‘Hasn’t Worked for a Year’ After Making Nolan’s Epic Because ‘I’m 49’ Years Old and ‘There’s Other Good Actors Out There’

title: Leslie Iwerks on ‘Disney Worldbuilders’ and How Jennifer Lee, James Cameron and Jared Bush Carry Forward Walt Disney’s Legacy
description: Filmmaker Leslie Iwerks is no stranger to pulling back the curtain on the magic of Disney. Her documentaries “The Pixar Story, “Disneyland Handcraft
body:
Filmmaker Leslie Iwerks is no stranger to pulling back the curtain on the magic of Disney. Her documentaries “The Pixar Story, “Disneyland Handcrafted” and “The Imagineering Story” all delve behind the scenes of the design and development processes that go into building Disney parks around the world.

	Her newest documentary, “Disney Worldbuilders,” premieres on Disney+ on Aug. 20. Bob Iger, James Cameron, Jon Favreau, Kevin Feige, Jennifer Lee, Pete Docter, Dave Filoni, Jared Bush and Josh D’Amaro anchor the narrative as they share behind-the-scenes moments that helped turn worlds like “Avatar,” “Star Wars,” the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Pixar, “Frozen” and “Zootopia” into Disney park experiences.
	



	

					Leslie Iwerks and Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige.
									MIKE TAING
	



	Disney is in Iwerks’ DNA. Her father, Donald Iwerks, spent over six decades on projects for The Walt Disney Company and his own studio, Iwerks Entertainment. He pioneered innovations in projection technology, 3D and large-format filmmaking, and immersive attractions that changed how audiences experience stories. Her grandfather, Ub Iwerks, cocreated Mickey Mouse, designing and drawing the iconic character while working alongside Walt Disney in 1928.


	Leslie Iwerks keeps Walt Disney’s saying, “Disneyland will never be completed, as long as there is imagination left in the world,” close to her heart and threads it through her storytelling. It was this quote that inspired her to profile this generation of imaginative thinkers. “They are the creators of these worlds that Walt started with,” she says of Cameron, Lee, Bush and the other subjects featured in the documentary. “They are continuing that lineage. I just thought it would be interesting to hear what excited them about creating their stories, their characters, and that evolution that now is in the parks as lands or as attractions.”
	

	One particularly touching moment in the documentary is when Iwerks follows Lee to Disneyland Paris ahead of the opening of World of Frozen.

	Lee wrote and co-directed “Frozen” and its 2019 sequel “Frozen 2.” In the documentary, Iwerks asks the creatives to share their early memories of the park. For Lee, it was Fantasyland. “She loved Cinderella, and she lived in that story as a kid, and so to film her at Disneyland Paris in Fantasyland, and then she speaks about how she and her sister were so close, and how that became the inspiration for ‘Frozen,’ and to see Jen in the world of ‘Frozen’ was so exciting,” says Iwerks.

	It’s a full-circle moment for Lee and her sister, who go on the “Frozen” ride together for the first time and see how Elsa and Anna come to life, knowing their own sisterly bond inspired the film. Iwerks says, “It was special.”

	The first time Lee saw the attraction was also an inspiring moment for her. “She had never walked in it before, and she’s so emotional. These are words on pages for her in her script and then to come up with these worlds, these places, and these moments, and then to see them in real life – that’s the gist of what Walt Disney wanted,” Iwerks explains. “He wanted to create characters that you can now experience live in the park.”

	Another important element of the storytelling is the passion of the creators. “They are all Disney fans first and foremost. They love the parks, and they grew up in the parks,” Iwerks says.

	One example of this is James Cameron, who sees the world of Pandora from his “Avatar” films come alive. Iwerks notes, “It’s fun to see these grown men who are still like kids in a way, and have that magic spark of Disney — it hasn’t left them.”

	Iwerks hopes in telling the story of “Disney Worldbuilders,” she will inspire the next generation of creators, world-builders, artists, and storytellers. “One thing I found fascinating was how much risk was involved in everyone’s story. Everyone had their struggles — Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks had their struggles, Disney and Roy had their struggles in building Disneyland — and those struggles continue. But it’s the passion and the desire to create joy that always gets them through. They’ll figure it out. That desire for detail, authenticity, and joy is what Walt started, and they’re continuing it.” She continues, “But with every creative endeavor, there’s always risk. What shines through is the passion everyone has to create.”

schema.headline: Leslie Iwerks on ‘Disney Worldbuilders’ and How Jennifer Lee, James Cameron and Jared Bush Carry Forward Walt Disney’s Legacy

Anna Kepner
                          Prosecutors Hand Over Her Snapchat Messages to Defense

                              August 4, 2026
                            5:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The prosecutors who are trying to put Anna Kepner’s step-brother behind bars for murder obtained her Snapchat data from her final days … and say they have now handed it over to his defense team … TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Court docs obtained by TMZ show prosecutors fired off a search warrant to obtain Anna’s messages and other info from her Snapchat and have now turned over the info to the defense.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The Snapchat messages are important because prosecutors have claimed Anna sent her final message on Snapchat at 8:14 p.m. The investigators say Anna’s brother Timothy Hudson, who was sharing the room with her, left the cabin at 10:13 PM and then returned at 11 PM.
      
    
            Timothy is facing charges over Anna’s death. Prosecutors claim Anna’s brother raped her and then killed her inside their cabin.

body:
Trump National Golf Course
                          Heavily Armed Man Arrested
                          ... Days Before Prez Set To Appear
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 4, 2026
                            5:26 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A man was arrested outside the Trump National Golf Club in California Sunday while allegedly monitoring "security-planning activities" ... just days before Donald Trump was set to headline a fundraiser there.
      
    
            Jeanine John Taele was allegedly taking pictures and walking the grounds when he was spotted by plainclothes federal agents ... multiple outlets report.
      
    
            When L.A. County Sheriff's Department deputies arrived, they found a loaded magazine in Taele's pocket. They also found a loaded pistol and more ammo in his car at the golf course parking lot.
      

            On Monday, authorities searched his home and found a ton of weapons ... including an illegally modified AR platform rifle, a .45-caliber pistol, body armor, high-capacity magazines and a even more ammo.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Taele was arrested on suspicion of carrying a concealed firearm and possessing prohibited ammunition.
      
    
            Trump is scheduled to appear at the golf course Tuesday night for a Republican National Committee fundraising dinner.

title: Hawaii Congressional Candidate Knocked Out Cold During Beach Fight, On Video

body:
Hawaiian Congressional Candidate
                          Gets His Ass Kicked During Beach Fight
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 4, 2026
                
                            1:09 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 4, 2026
                                4:07 PM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
          UPDATE
  
    
            2:05 PM PT -- Maui Police Department tells TMZ ... at one point, Kirill Basin had pulled out a knife -- injuring himself in the process.
      
    
            He allegedly chucked it into the ocean before the cops arrived. They say a bystander found the alleged knife and turned it over to police.
      
    
            MPD tells us the whole thing started when Basin was approached about turning his music down ... they say he allegedly threatened the man and his wife, claiming he had a gun and was going to shoot her.
      
    
            A Hawaiian congressional candidate got hit by a double whammy ... he first got his ass whooped on the beach ... and then he reportedly got arrested for making terroristic threats ... and the brawl is on video.
      
    
            Kirill Basin, a Democratic candidate running for Congress against incumbent Democrat Jill Tokuda, got into a heated back-and-forth Saturday with a couple at Keawakapu Beach on Maui. The verbal altercation was captured by a witness on dramatic video, along with the ensuing ass-kicking.
      
    
          Waiting for your permission to load TikTok Post.
      
    
            Check it out and bring the popcorn ... the clip starts with Basin talking about putting the other man in the hospital before doing a total 180 and shaking the man's hand.
      

            But then Basin tells the man's female companion to go f*** herself -- and that's when everything goes off the rails.
      
    
            In the end, Basin gets knocked out cold by a single punch thrown by the other man. The politician drops like a sack of potatoes, and some guy starts slapping his face to wake him up while he's unconscious on the ground.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            After cops arrived, things only got worse for Basin, who was arrested for 2 counts of terroristic threatening in the first degree ... and his bail was set at $1 million -- MPD tells TMZ.
      
    
            The news site reports a 61-year-old man asked Basin to turn down the volume on the music he was playing. Basin allegedly implied he had a gun and would shoot his wife, sparking the physical altercation.
      
    
            During the fight, Basin allegedly produced a knife and threatened a bunch of people with it before he got knocked into next week.
